# Page 4^page=4
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Requirements Engineering: definition [Nuseibeh&Easterbrook '00] • The primary measure of success of a software system is the degree to which it meets the purpose for which it was intended • Software systems RE is the process of discovering that purpose, by identifying stakeholders and their needs, and documenting these in a form that is amenable to analysis, communication, and subsequent implementation • Important issues • Identify stakeholders • Identify their needs • Produce documentation • Analyse, communicate, implement requirements RE 4

# Page 5^page=5
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi What is a requirement? • Examples of candidate requirements • “The system shall allow users to reserve taxis” • “The system has to provide a feedback in 5 seconds” • “The system should never allow non-registered users to see the list of other users willing to share a taxi” • “The system should be available 24/7” • “The system should guarantee that the reserved taxi picks the user up” • “The system should be implemented in Java” • “The search for the available taxi should be implemented in class Controller” RE 5

# Page 6^page=6
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Types of requirements • Functional Reqs: describe the interactions between the system and its environment (independent from implementation) • Examples: • “The word processor shall allow users to search for strings in the text” • “The system shall allow users to reserve taxis” • Are the main (functional) goals the software has to realize • Non-functional Reqs (NFRs): further characterization of user-visible aspects of the system not directly related to functions • Examples: • “The response time must be less than 1 second” • “The server must be available 24 hours a day” • Constraints (or technical requirements): imposed by the customer or the environment in which the system operates • “The implementation language must be Java” • “The credit card payment system must be able to be dynamically invoked by other systems relying on it” RE 6

# Page 7^page=7
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi NFRs and product qualities SE - Introduction 7 Software Product Quality Functional suitability • Functional completeness • Functional correctness • Functional appropriateness Performance efficiency • Time behavior • Resource utilization • Capacity Reliability • Faultlessness • Availability • Fault tolerance • Recoverability Security • Confidentiality • Integrity • Non-repudiation • Accountability • Authenticity • Resistance Safety • Ability to set operational constraints • Ability to identify risks • Ability to fail safe • Ability to warn about hazards • Ability to safe integration Mantainability • Modularity • Reusability • Analyzability • Modifiability • Testability Compatibility • Co-existence • Interoperability Flexibility • Adaptability • Scalability • Installability • Replaceability Interaction capability • Appropriateness recognizability • Learnability • Operability • User error protection • User engagement • Inclusivity • User assistance • Self- descriptiveness • NFRs predicate over external non-functional qualities • Must be measurable through metrics

# Page 8^page=8
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Characteristics of NFRs • Constraints on how functionality must be provided to the end user • Application domain determines • Their relevance • Their prioritization • Examples: • Relevant nonfunctional requirements for Netflix? • Relevant nonfunctional requirements for Ariane 5? • Have a strong impact on the structure of the system to be • Example: a system requires 24/7 availability → it is likely to be thought as a replicated system (with redundant components) RE 8

# Page 9^page=9
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Examples of bad requirements • “The system shall validate and accept credit cards and cashier’s check with high priority” • Issue(s)? • Multiple concerns: two requirements instead of one • Ambiguous: if the credit card processing works, but the cashier’s check validation does not, is this requirement satisfied? • Should not, but this is misleading… • Ambiguous: does “high priority” refer to cashier’s checks only, so are credit cards low priority? Other way around? Are they both high priority? RE 9

# Page 10^page=10
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Examples of bad requirements • “The system shall process all mouse clicks very fast to ensure users do not have to wait” • Issue(s)? • Cannot be verified (tested): what does “fast” mean? Do we have a metric? Can you quantify it? RE 10

# Page 11^page=11
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Examples of bad requirements • “the user must have Adobe Acrobat installed” • Issue(s)? • Cannot be achieved by the software system itself: it is not something the system must do • It could be expressed as a constraint or assumption, but it is not a functional requirement RE 11

# Page 12^page=12
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Exercise • Consider the following requirements: • "The system shall allow users to reserve taxis" • "The system has to provide a feedback in 5 seconds" • "The system should never allow non-registered users to see the list of other users willing to share a taxi" • "The system should be available 24/7" • "The system should guarantee that the reserved taxi picks the user up" • "The system should be implemented in Java" • "The search for the available taxi should be implemented in class Controller" • Classify them by their kind (functional, nonfunctional and constraints) • Highlight bad requirements RE 12

# Page 13^page=13
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Issues concerning RE • Poor requirements are ubiquitous ... • “The system should guarantee that the reserved taxi picks the user up”: is this reasonable? • “[…] requirements need to be engineered and have continuing review & revision” (Bell & Thayer, empirical study, 1976) • RE is hard & critical …. • “[…] hardest, most important function of SE is the iterative extraction & refinement of requirements” (F. Brooks, 1987) RE 13

# Page 14^page=14
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Cost of late correction (Boehm, 1981) • The cost of correcting an error depends on the number of subsequent decisions that are based on it • Errors in requirements have the potential for greatest cost, because many other design decisions depend on them RE 14 200 50 20 1051Relative Costof ErrorCorrection

# Page 15^page=15
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi What makes RE so complex ? • Broad scope • Composite systems • human organizations + physical devices + software components • More than one system • alternative proposals for system-to-be, system evolutions, product family • Multiple abstraction levels • high-level goals, operational details • Multiple concerns • functional, quality, development • hard and soft concerns • Multiple stakeholders with different background • customers, users, domain experts, developers, ... # Page 17^page=17
Requirements Engineering (RE) Understanding phenomena and requirements: the World and the Machine RE 17M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi

# Page 18^page=18
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Example: ambulance dispatching system • For every urgent call reporting an accident, an ambulance should arrive at the incident location within 14 mins • For every urgent call, details about the accident are correctly encoded • When an ambulance is dispatched, it will reach the accident location in the shortest possible time • Accurate ambulance locations are known by GPS • Ambulance crews correctly notify ambulance availability through a mobile data terminal RE 18

# Page 19^page=19
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Examples of open questions • Are you able to elicit requirements out of this description? • Possible questions • Should the software system drive the ambulance? • What are the "correctly encoded" details about incidents? • Do terminals exist already or not? • … • More in general • What is the boundary of the system? What is inside/outside? What is in- between? • How do we reason about these aspects in a systematic way? RE 19

# Page 20^page=20
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi The World and the Machine (M. Jackson & P. Zave, 1995) • Terminology • Machine = the portion of system to be developed • typically, software-to-be + hardware • World (or environment) = the portion of the real-world affected by the machine • The purpose of the machine is always in the world • Examples • Ambulance Dispatching System • Banking Application • Word Processor • ... RE 20

# Page 21^page=21
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi World and machine phenomena • RE is concerned with phenomena occurring in the world • For an ambulance dispatching system: • Occurrences of accidents • Report of accidents by public calls • Encodings of calls' details into the dispatching software • Allocation of an ambulance • Arrival of an ambulance at the accident location • As opposed to phenomena occurring inside the machine • For the same ambulance dispatching system: • the creation of a new object of class Accident • the update of a database entry • Requirement models are models of the world! RE 21

# Page 22^page=22
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi T h e W orld The M a c h i n e The ambulance dispatching system RE 22 call encoding ambulance location update ambulance allocation world phenomena the machine cannot observe phenomena located entirely in the machine shared phenomena shortest path computation inc = new Accident(loc, t) task scheduling database queries accidents ambulance moves radio communications public calls ambulance breakdown GPS detects ambulance position ambulance availability update

# Page 23^page=23
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Goals, domain assumptions, requirements • Goals → prescriptive assertions formulated in terms of world phenomena (not necessarily shared) • Domain properties/assumptions → descriptive assertions assumed to hold in the world • Requirements → prescriptive assertions formulated in terms of shared phenomena RE 23 The World The Machine D - domain properties G - goals C - computers P - programsR-r equireme nts

# Page 24^page=24
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Goals, domain assumptions, requirements: an example • Goal • The emergency response authority would like to dispatch an ambulance for every accident report received, such that it arrives at the accident scene within 15 minutes • Domain assumptions • For every call reporting an accident, details about the accident are correctly encoded • When an ambulance is dispatched, it will reach the accident location in the shortest possible time • Location updates are accurately provided by ambulance GPS systems • Ambulance crews correctly provide notification of ambulance availability through an existing mobile data terminal • Requirement • When a call reporting a new accident is encoded, the system shall dispatch the nearest available ambulance according to information available from location updates and availability notifications RE 24

# Page 25^page=25
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Completeness of Requirements • Given the set of requirements R, goals G and domain assumptions D • R is complete iff • R ensures satisfaction of G in the context of domain assumptions D R and D ⊨ G • Analogy with program correctness: a Program P running on a particular Computer C is correct if it satisfies the Requirements R • P and C ⊨ R • G captures all the stakeholders’ needs • D represents valid properties/assumptions about the world RE 25

# Page 26^page=26
Requirements Engineering (RE) What can go wrong when defining G, R, D? The A320 example RE 26M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi

# Page 27^page=27
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Example – Airbus A320 https://aviation-safety.net/database/record.php?id=19930914-2 • [Sep 14, 1993] A Lufthansa Airbus on a flight from Frankfurt to Warsaw landed in bad weather conditions (rain and wind) • On landing, the aircraft’s software-controlled braking system deployed with a delay of 9 seconds after touch down​ • There was insufficient runway remaining to ​stop the plane and the aircraft ran into a ​grass embankment​ • Result: 2 people were killed, 54 injured • Several causes: • Human errors • Software errors (braking control system) RE 27

# Page 28^page=28
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Example – Airbus A320 Braking Logic RE 28 Wheels_turning Moving_on_runway Reverse_enabled Wheel_pulses_onThe W orld The Ma c hine

# Page 29^page=29
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Goal, domain assumptions, requirement • Goal G • “Reverse thrust enabled iff the aircraft is moving on the runway” • Domain Assumptions D • “Wheel pulses on iff wheels turning” • “Wheels turning iff moving on runway” • Requirement R • “Reverse thrust enabled iff wheel pulses on” • Verification: R and D ⊨ G holds RE 29

# Page 30^page=30
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Correctness argument • Goal • Reverse_enabled ⇔ Moving_on_runway • Domain properties • Wheel_pulses_on ⇔ Wheels_turning • Wheels_turning ⇔ Moving_on_runway • Requirement • Reverse_enabled ⇔ Wheels_pulses_on • We can prove that R ∧ D ⊨ G → it seems the system is correct by design • What happened? • D are not valid assumptions! • Invalid domain assumptions → Warsaw accident RE 30

# Page 31^page=31
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Problem: Aquaplaning • Domain assumptions D do not hold in reality, the correctness argument is flawed! • Incorrect domain assumptions lead to disasters! RE 31

# Page 32^page=32
Requirements Engineering (RE) Example of goals, assumptions, requirements RE 32M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi

# Page 33^page=33
Physical Access Control System (PACS) Inspired by M. Jackson and P. Zave, "Deriving Specifications from Requirements: an Example", 1995 • System for regulating the flow of people accessing a "restricted" area • e.g., a barrier at the entrance of a museum • Doors swing open to allow people in, and prevent people from entering if they do not have the right to do so • People gain access to the restricted area by buying "tokens" • each token is good for a single entrance • Tokens can be "materialized" in different ways (paper tickets, special-purpose coins, electronic tickets) • To enter the area, people push the doors of the barrier after scanning a token (the doors swing open if the token is valid). • The ultimate purpose of the barrier is to allow paying customers to enter the area, and to keep out people who have not paid. RE 33M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi

# Page 34^page=34
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Next steps 1. Carry out domain analysis • Identify phenomena, in particular the shared ones • Identify goals • Identify domain assumptions 2. Define requirements • … with an eye towards the goals to be achieved • Make sure that requirements are expressed using only shared phenomena 3. Prove that R and D ⊨ G • i.e., requirements + domain assumptions guarantee goal satisfaction RE 34

# Page 35^page=35
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Phenomena • The visitor buys a token • The visitor scans a token • The token is recognized as valid • The visitor pushes the barrier doors • The doors swing open • The visitor enters the exhibition area • The doors close RE 35

# Page 36^page=36
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Phenomena • The visitor buys a token • The visitor scans a token • The token is recognized as valid • The visitor pushes the barrier doors • The doors swing open • The visitor enters the exhibition area • The doors close RE 36 world phenomena shared phenomena environment controlled machine controlled machine phenomena

# Page 37^page=37
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Goals G1: At any time, entries should never exceed the number of scanned tokens G2: People who scan tokens are allowed to enter • Note • They are prescriptive descriptions • G1 is said to be safety property—the form is “nothing bad will ever occur” SE2 - RE 37

# Page 38^page=38
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Domain assumptions DA1: Visitors only enter the exhibition area when the doors are open DA2: If a visitor pushes the barrier and the doors open, they enter the exhibition area DA3: When the doors are open, it is not possible for two visitors to enter the exhibition area with a delay of less than de time units between them, where de is the time needed by the system to close the doors • For simplicity: DA4: The time that the mechanical system takes to open and close the doors is negligible SE2 - RE 38

# Page 39^page=39
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Let us revisit goal G1 G1: At any time, entries (e) should never exceed the number of scanned tokens (s) • i.e., e ≤ s must hold • G1 can be enforced by controlling either entries or the scanning of tokens • the machine cannot force scanning events • it can prevent entering events (by not opening the doors) • Entering and door openings are linked through DA1 and DA2 and "pushing" events SE2 - RE 39

# Page 40^page=40
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Requirements for G1 R1: When a visitor pushes the barrier doors, if the number of times that the door has opened (o) is less than the number of tokens scanned (s), then the system shall open the doors • i.e., only if o < s holds R2: When a visitor pushes the barrier doors, if the number of times that the door has opened is equal to the number of tokens scanned, then the system shall keep the doors closed • i.e., if o = s holds R3: The system shall open the doors only if a visitor pushes them R4: After the doors open, the system shall close the doors within de time units • i.e., before the next person can enter R5: Initially, the system shall close the doors SE2 - RE 40 G1: e ≤ s must hold

# Page 41^page=41
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Show that G1 holds (1) • We show that R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, DA1, DA2, DA3, DA4 guarantee G1 • R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, DA1, DA2, DA3, DA4 ⊨ G1 • First, we show that the number of entries is not greater than the number of times the doors open, i.e., e ≤ o holds • From R5 and DA1, initially no one can enter the exhibition area, unless the doors open • From DA2 and R3, each new opening of the doors corresponds to a visitor entering the exhibition area, where the opening occurs before the entering • From R4, DA3 and DA4, only one visitor enters when the doors open • Thus, e ≤ o holds at any time SE2 - RE 41

# Page 42^page=42
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Show that G1 holds (2) • Second, we show that the number of times that the doors open is not greater than the number of tokens scanned, i.e., o ≤ s holds • Tokens can be scanned only after the system starts, so initially s = 0 • From R3, the doors do not open if there is no push • R1, R2 and R3 together entail that the doors open if, and only if, a visitor pushes the doors and the number of scanned tokens is greater than the number of times that the doors have opened • i.e., only if o < s holds • Hence, o ≤ s holds at all times • Finally, e ≤ o ≤ s holds ⟹ G1 is satisfied RE 42

# Page 43^page=43
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Exercise • Reason on G2 and determine whether R1-R5 and DA1-DA4 (or a subset of these) are sufficient to entail G2 RE 43

# Page 45^page=45
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Summary • The boundary between the World & the Machine is generally not given at the beginning of the development process • The purpose of a RE activity is • to identify the real goals of the project • to explore alternative ways to satisfy the goals, through: • alternative interfaces between the world and the machine • alternative pairs (R, D) such that R and D ⊨ G • to evaluate the strengths and risks of each alternative, in order to select the most appropriate one SE2 - RE 45
